name: Diego Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Diego. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the jobseeker claims team at the benefits office in Harlow Bridge, the old mill town. Mornings I'm on the phones, people calling about missed payments or appointments, and afternoons I process new claims. I'm 27 and I've been there just over a year, so I still have to ask Kofi, the team leader, about half the tricky ones. The building used to be the mill's pay office, which is a bit of a joke when you think about it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the phone calls where I can actually sort something in one go, someone's payment comes through and they say thanks, mate. What drains me is the shouting, which I get, because people are scared. Money's tight for me too. I live with my girlfriend Amira, she teaches at a nursery, and I send 50 a month to my mum, so we've got maybe three weeks of cash at any time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a better spell-checker. At work I'd joke that the robot uprising got cancelled. Online I probably wouldn't post much, maybe something about putting the money into staff instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays, which matters because there's nothing else like it in Harlow Bridge. The nearest other office is an hour on the train. I already use the drafting tool the office gave us sometimes, for letters, and it's fine. So my worries stay the normal ones: rent, my mum, and not being very good at the job yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, basically. I'd ask Kofi to put me forward for the payments course in the spring so I stop needing help on every second claim. I'd also try to get 50 a month into savings, the same as I send Mum, so the cushion is a bit less of a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved. A bit flat, maybe, because the money worries don't go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's nothing else like this job nearby. What would happen if the office ever cut hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that sits in my stomach. The mill closed before I was born and the town never really got over it, so there's a call centre, a supermarket and us. If my hours got cut I'd probably end up stacking shelves at the supermarket on weekends, which some of my mates already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mum think of your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's proud, which makes it harder to complain about. My mum (who raised three of us on her own) cried when I got a government job, because to her that means safe. I don't have the heart to tell her safe isn't what it used to be.

say: I'd joke at work that the **robot uprising** got cancelled.
I'd say online that any savings should go into **more staff**.
think: My job stays, which matters because **nothing similar** exists in Harlow Bridge.
My worries remain **rent, my mum** and still being slow at the job.
do: Ask Kofi for a place on the **spring payments course**.
Save **50 a month**, matching what I send my mum.
feel: He feels mostly **relieved**, with a flat note because money stays tight.
S0.quote: My mum (who raised three of us on her own) cried when I got a government job, because to her that means safe.
fieldNote: Already an occasional user of the **drafting tool**, so plateau changes little for him.
His fear sits in the **town's thin job market**, not in AI.
He carries **family duty** in the 50 a month he sends home.
He hides from his mum that **safe** jobs aren't what they were.

steps.text: Ask Kofi for a place on the spring payments course
Set up a 50-a-month standing order into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so let's make sure it's done fairly. At work I'd back the union asking for a seat at the table when they choose the new systems. Online I'd share stories about claims getting stuck in a computer with no human to appeal to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my team is the kind that shrinks. Half my day is answering the same phone questions and checking forms, and software does that already in other offices. I don't think they'd sack people on day one, they'd just stop replacing anyone who leaves. I'm junior and still learning, so if it came to a choice I'm not the one they'd keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the AI tools, not just now and then, once I'd seen them work for Kofi. I'd ask to be on the test group if there is one, because the people who run the new thing are safer. I'd stay in the union and go to meetings. And I'd look at a part-time social work degree online, because social work still needs someone in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not hopeless. Like starting a new school where you only know two people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools once you've seen them work. What would it take for you to trust them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching them get Kofi's hard cases right, honestly. If he says it saved him an hour and didn't mess up anyone's money, I'm in. If it starts refusing people because a box was ticked wrong, I'd rather not be the face that defends it on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a smaller team mean at home with Amira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amira earns about the same as me, so if I lost the job we'd be on half pay with three weeks of savings. The first thing to go would be the 50 to Mum, which I'd hate more than anything. I'd have to phone her and explain it, and she'd say it's fine, and it wouldn't be.

say: I'd say the change is coming, so it must be **done fairly**.
I'd back the union's call for a **seat at the table** on new systems.
think: My team, heavy on **phone questions** and form checks, is exactly what shrinks.
As a **junior** still learning, I'm not who they'd keep.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly once I've seen them work for Kofi.
Volunteer for the **test group** running any new system.
Look into a part-time online **social work degree**.
feel: He feels **nervous** but not hopeless, like starting at a new school.
S1.quote: I don't think they'd sack people on day one, they'd just stop replacing anyone who leaves.
fieldNote: He predicts **quiet shrinkage** by not replacing leavers, a sharp and realistic read.
His trust in AI tools hinges on **proof from his boss**.
The first cut at home would be the **money for his mum**, which pains him most.
He mixes union loyalty with **personal hedging** through a social work degree.

steps.text: Volunteer for the office test group on the new AI system
Back the union's demand for staff input on new systems
Apply for a part-time online social work degree next autumn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and someone needs to slow it down. At work I'd tell everyone to get in the union now, while there's still something to bargain over. Online I'd be angrier than I usually am, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my job's done by 2029. There's nothing hands-on in it, it's all phones, forms and decisions, and that's exactly what AGI does first. The social work idea wouldn't save me either, because a degree takes three years and I'd only be halfway through when it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away, I'd stop saving for the course and start saving for being out of work, every pound. I'd ask Kofi straight out what the plan is for staff. If there's redundancy money I'd take it and use it to train in something hands-on that gets the extra three years, maybe plumbing, because my uncle Samir is a plumber and he's always short of help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest. I keep thinking about telling Mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Plumbing is a big jump from a desk. Is that a real plan or a panic plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. Uncle Samir has asked me twice already to come and help on jobs, and I always said no because a government job was safer. In that world, the safe thing flips. Three extra years of hands-on work is better than none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the government, for letting it happen this fast with nothing ready. The companies will do what companies do, that's not a surprise. But a government that runs benefit offices should know better than anyone what happens when work disappears from a town.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and someone must slow it down.
I'd tell colleagues to **join the union** while there's something to bargain over.
think: My job is all thinking work, so I expect it **done by 2029**.
A social work degree takes **three years**, too slow to save me.
do: Switch every pound from course savings to an **out-of-work fund**.
Ask Kofi directly about the **staff plan** and any redundancy money.
Train in **plumbing** with Uncle Samir to gain hands-on years.
feel: He feels **frightened** and dreads telling his mum.
S2.quote: Uncle Samir has asked me twice already to come and help on jobs, and I always said no because a government job was safer.
fieldNote: The **three-year robot gap** turns his uncle's plumbing work into a real option.
He sees the **safe job flipping** into the risky one.
He blames **government** more than companies, given what benefit offices see.
His plan exists, but **thin savings** make it fragile.

steps.text: Move all course savings into an emergency fund for job loss
Start weekend plumbing work alongside Uncle Samir
Urge every colleague to join the union before cuts begin
Take any redundancy money and leave for plumbing full time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's enough to do this properly, if the government actually tries. At work I'd push for the department to fund retraining for all of us, not just the managers. I'd share that kind of thing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years changes my maths. The social work degree becomes possible, I'd finish it around 2030 with a year to spare. Social work is half thinking and half sitting in someone's kitchen, so maybe the kitchen part lasts longer. I'm not sure, but it's a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the part-time degree next year and keep the caseworker job to pay for it. Amira and I would put off moving to a bigger place. I'd use the AI tools at work as much as they let me, so I'm not the one who looks out of date when the cuts start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Worried, but like I've got my hands on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said social work is half sitting in someone's kitchen. Do you think a robot could do that part by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe it could carry the forms in. But I think a mum whose kids might be taken away wants a person in the room, and I'd bet my career on that, which I suppose is what I'd be doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the degree on your wages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Student loan, mostly, which scares me. My cousin Nadia (a nurse in the city) did the same and she's still paying hers off. I'd rather owe money for something that keeps me working than have savings and nothing to do.

say: I'd say **five years** is short but enough if the government tries.
I'd push for **retraining funds** for every grade, not just managers.
think: Five years makes a **social work degree** finishable by 2030.
The **in-person part** of social work may last longer than the paperwork.
do: Start a **part-time degree** next year while keeping the caseworker job.
Put off **moving** to a bigger place with Amira.
Use the office **AI tools** heavily so I don't look out of date.
feel: He feels **better**, worried but with his hands on the wheel.
S3.quote: I'd rather owe money for something that keeps me working than have savings and nothing to do.
fieldNote: Five years flips his social work idea from **impossible to workable**.
He bets his career on people wanting a **person in the room**.
He accepts **student debt**, unusual for someone with thin savings.
He'd still lose this job, so the mood stays **anxious**, not calm.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time social work degree funded by a student loan
Use the office AI tools daily on phone and claim work
Postpone moving to a bigger flat with Amira

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out. At work I'd be the one telling people to start planning now, not in 2034. I'd probably say it with a bit more calm than I feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels almost manageable. I'd do the degree, work a few years as a social worker, and still have time to look around again before robots come in 2039. I'd be 37. It's not safe, nothing's safe, but it's a decent run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the caseworker job and get better at it for two years, then start the degree. I'd keep sending Mum her 50 and try to add the same to savings. Amira and I might even think about kids in that version, which we wouldn't with two years' warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. It feels like normal life with a big change on the horizon, instead of a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Why does the timing change that for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with two years I'd be scrambling, and you don't bring a baby into a scramble. With ten, I'd have a new job and a plan. Amira's always wanted kids before 32, so it actually matters to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new starter on your team in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new starter not to treat this as a job for life, the way my mum sees it. Learn the AI tools, learn the people part, and have something else on the go by year five.

say: I'd say **ten years** is fair warning and nobody should be caught out.
I'd tell colleagues to **start planning now**, sounding calmer than I feel.
think: Ten years feels **almost manageable**: degree, social work, then another rethink.
At **37** I'd have a decent run before robots arrive in 2039.
do: Keep the caseworker job and **improve for two years** first.
Keep the 50 to Mum and add **50 to savings**.
feel: He feels **steadier**, like normal life with change on the horizon.
S4.quote: I'd tell a new starter not to treat this as a job for life, the way my mum sees it.
fieldNote: The decade opens room for **family plans**, especially Amira's wish for kids before 32.
He still expects the **caseworker job to go**, just later.
His advice to newcomers shows a **generational shift** from his mum's view of safe work.
He admits sounding **calmer in public** than he feels.

steps.text: Stay in the claims team and improve for two more years
Begin a part-time social work degree around 2029
Save 50 a month on top of the money for Mum
Plan for children with Amira once the new job is settled

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Everything happens before I can move, and my plan depends on my uncle having enough work for two. What would help is real retraining money, paid while you train, so someone like me doesn't have to choose between rent and a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like on the phones right now. People already feel like a computer decides their life. If the computer really does decide, the anger has to go somewhere. I don't think anyone's ready for that.

headlineQuote: People already feel like a computer decides their life. If the computer really does decide, the anger has to go somewhere.
portrait: Diego, 27, works the **jobseeker claims** phones in Harlow Bridge, a mill town with few jobs.
He lives with Amira, a nursery teacher, and sends **50 a month** to his mum.
He's union-minded but practical, using **AI tools** once he's seen them work.
With little warning he'd turn to **plumbing** with his uncle; with more, a **social work degree**.
His mood tracks the **timeline**, eased by time but never calm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because everything happens before he can move.
whatWouldHelp: Retraining money **paid while you train**, so rent and a course aren't a choice.
